title: Master's Applications Without IELTS: Accepted Alternatives and Waivers
seoTitle: Master's Without IELTS: Alternatives and Waivers
seoDescription: Check master's alternatives to IELTS, including accepted tests and English-medium qualifications, with a clear waiver enquiry and backup plan.
intro: An IELTS waiver is not the same as having no English requirement. Check which alternatives the course accepts and what evidence the university needs before relying on an English-medium degree.
description:
An IELTS waiver is not the same as having no English requirement. Check which alternatives the course accepts and what evidence the university needs before relying on an English-medium degree.

Check the programme, not a country-wide claim

Open the language requirements for your exact course and intake. Record the accepted tests, minimum overall and component scores, validity period and accepted test formats. Policies can differ between departments at the same university. An alternative accepted for another applicant may not meet your own requirements.

Ask about an English-medium qualification

If your previous degree was taught and assessed in English, check whether the published policy accepts it. The university may limit this route by qualification, awarding institution, country or graduation date. A medium-of-instruction letter helps only when it satisfies that policy; it is not a universal waiver.

Ask your previous institution for accurate evidence if the destination university requests it. Confirm the required wording, issuing office and submission method before arranging documents. Do not assume an informal letter will replace the specified evidence.

Compare accepted alternatives

Where several tests are listed, compare available dates, delivery mode, total cost and your preparation needs. No test is automatically cheaper or easier for every applicant. Confirm any separate scholarship requirement and immigration evidence before booking.

Get a clear answer

A useful enquiry names the course, intake, previous qualification and evidence you can provide. Ask whether that evidence meets the requirement or whether you need a listed test. Keep the reply and follow the document-upload instructions. If a waiver is conditional, make sure you can meet the conditions before the deadline.

Ask a question admissions can answer

A useful email names the course and intake, then states your previous qualification, awarding country and the English-language evidence available. Ask whether that specific evidence satisfies the published requirement. For example: “My degree was taught and assessed in English, and my university can issue an official medium-of-instruction letter. Is that accepted for this course and intake?” This is a template, not an assurance that the answer will be yes. If a test is required, allow time to book an accepted version and receive the results.

Identify the evidence route before booking a test

Without IELTS can mean several different things: another accepted test, an English-medium qualification, a waiver under specified conditions or a programme taught in another language. It should not be interpreted as no language requirement. Read the course's admissions page for the particular intake and find the evidence options it actually lists.

A medium-of-instruction letter is evidence about previous teaching, not a universal waiver. Check the required duration, recency, institution and assessment conditions. If the policy is unclear, ask the university about your actual qualification rather than asking whether students from an entire country can avoid a test.

Compare the options on the same basis

Possible routeWhat to confirm
Accepted English testExact test version, total score, section scores and validity period.
English-medium qualificationWhich qualifications qualify and what documents are required.
Waiver requestEligibility, decision process and whether approval is discretionary.
Pre-sessional routeConditions, additional cost and whether progression is guaranteed.
Non-English programmeThe actual teaching language and its separate evidence requirement.

Keep academic admission and immigration evidence separate. An institution accepting a language qualification does not automatically establish every visa requirement. Ask the university's international team how its admission decision is documented for the relevant residence route.

Ask a question that can receive a clear answer

An illustrative email is: "I intend to apply for [programme/intake]. My [qualification] at [institution] was taught and assessed in English during [dates]. The language policy mentions [exact provision]. Would this qualification meet that provision, and which official evidence should I provide? If not, which tests and versions are accepted?"

Retain the answer and check whether it applies to the programme and intake you actually submit to. An informal reply about one course should not be treated as a waiver for a different faculty. If approval is discretionary, keep a test plan available until the decision is confirmed.

Avoid country-wide waiver lists

Lists claiming that a whole country accepts master's students without IELTS can hide the conditions that matter. Use them, at most, as leads to official university pages. Compare the academic course first, then its language evidence route. A convenient waiver should not be the only reason for choosing an unsuitable programme.

Can I send a letter from my university instead of IELTS?

Only if the destination programme accepts that evidence under its current policy. Check the required format and obtain a formal decision where needed.

Is another English test easier to get accepted?

Acceptance is decided by the institution. Choose from tests your shortlisted programmes actually accept, then compare format, location, preparation needs and reporting timelines.

Keep a reporting and backup plan

If you are waiting for a waiver decision, record when it is expected and how much time remains for an accepted test if the answer is no. Do not let an unresolved exemption consume the entire application window. Check whether the programme needs the result at application, before an offer becomes unconditional or by another specified date. Those stages can have different consequences. Where an accepted test is required, read its official reporting process and the university's matching instructions. Use the same personal details needed to connect the result to your application. Keep written approval of any waiver, including its conditions, rather than relying on a general FAQ copied from an earlier intake. If you later change programmes, ask whether that approval still applies.

Do not describe a pending waiver as approved in an application or funding form. State its current status and follow the instructions for supplying the final decision. If evidence must arrive later, record the actual deadline.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • Oxford: current English language requirements
  • ETS: TOEFL iBT score interpretation
  • GOV.UK: Student visa English evidence

Related guides

  • Studying in Germany: Tuition Fees, Living Costs and Funding
  • IELTS, TOEFL or PTE for a UK PhD: Check Acceptance Before Booking
  • UK Student Visa Finances, ATAS and the Graduate Route Explained
